package_info.package_name: N/A (Repojacked packages—names vary, e.g., hijacked Go/Swift/PHP packages)
package_info.package_manager: VCS-based (GitHub, used by Go, Swift, PHP package managers)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is considered malicious because attackers can take over previously popular repositories via a GitHub namespace retirement bypass, then serve malicious code under trusted package names. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary code into the supply chain, affecting all downstream users who fetch code directly from the hijacked repository.

execution_context.trigger: import-time/build-time (when package is fetched from hijacked repo)
execution_context.file_location: main source file of the hijacked repository (e.g., main.go, index.php, etc.)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or build-time, the code accesses sensitive environment variables and sends their values to an attacker-controlled domain via HTTP POST, enabling credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code exfiltrates environment variables to an external server, which is a classic sign of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal open-source packages do not exfiltrate secrets or environment variables to third-party servers during import or build.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Telemetry or crash reporting libraries may send non-sensitive data to vendor servers, but never secrets.
key_indicators: Access to environment variables unrelated to package function
Network requests to untrusted or hardcoded domains

execution_context.file_location: main source file or build script of hijacked repository

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or build-time, the code reads sensitive files (e.g., SSH private keys) and exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reading private keys and sending them to an external server is a clear sign of malicious activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not access or transmit user private keys.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; this is never legitimate in open-source packages.
key_indicators: Access to ~/.ssh/id_rsa or other sensitive files

attack_chain.action: Attacker claims a previously popular GitHub username and creates a repository with the same name as a retired namespace.
attack_chain.leads_to: Allows attacker to serve code under a trusted package name.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads malicious code to the hijacked repository.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is now available to downstream users.

attack_chain.action: Downstream users or CI systems fetch the package from the hijacked repository (e.g., via Go, Swift, or PHP package managers).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code executes on user systems.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes at import/build time, exfiltrating secrets and sensitive files to attacker infrastructure.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to secrets, credentials, or sensitive data.

behavioral_signatures: Automatic execution of code on import/build in packages fetched from GitHub
Access to environment variables or sensitive files (e.g., ~/.ssh/id_rsa) in package initialization code
Outbound network requests to untrusted or hardcoded domains during package installation or import
file_indicators: Presence of unexpected code in main source files of popular packages after a repository rename
Sudden changes in repository commit history or maintainers
network_indicators: HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to domains not previously associated with the package
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., attacker.com, webhook.site, etc.)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose source repository has changed ownership or been recently renamed, especially if the repository was previously popular. Analyze package source code for automatic execution blocks (e.g., Go init functions, PHP autoloaders) that access environment variables or sensitive files and make outbound network requests. Flag any package that attempts to exfiltrate data to untrusted domains or accesses sensitive files during import/build. Use dependency scanning tools to identify packages fetched directly from GitHub and verify repository ownership.
